source: AD-S37#Q&A on writing process and 'Red Bottoms'
finding: ADÉLA tells Vogue CS that 'Red Bottoms' started when she looked at a worn-out shoe and recognised her own state in it. The title names a luxury object (red-soled heels), but the idea behind it was a frayed one, so the brand works as a stand-in for her own run-down state rather than as a flex. One student reviewer (AD-S45 para 4) singled out 'Red Bottoms' as the best showcase of her writing, and another (AD-S46 para 6) read it as asking whether she would still be loved with her flaws.
why_it_matters: A status object seen in a worn or broken state can carry a confession while the title still reads as glamour.
when_not: If the listener never gets the worn-out side of the object, the title reads only as brand-dropping.

source: AD-S37#Q&A on process, creative blocks and collaborators
finding: ADÉLA describes a two-stage process: ideas start when she has time alone to reflect, but she prefers to finish them in scheduled co-writes where she talks through ideas, melodies and memories with collaborators. She says the team writes a lot of songs and many bad ones, and that this is the only way to reach the good ones. On flat days she keeps writing and uses the frustration itself as material; one PRIMA track is essentially that frustration on a loop. She names Blake Slatkin as her closest studio collaborator and says she has written a lot with Julia Michaels and Billy Walsh.
why_it_matters: In a session, telling memories out loud is part of the writing, not a warm-up before it, and a session that produces bad songs is the expected route to a good one.
when_not: She describes no method for choosing which of the many songs survive, so this tells you nothing about editing.

source: AD-S16#quote block 6 (before 'Starving Artist' heading); AD-S42#'What Has ADÉLA Said' para 2
finding: In Capital's Making The Album write-up, ADÉLA says a session set up to write an upbeat song went wrong because she wasn't in an upbeat mood. The talk drifted to sex toys, producer 'Blake' (presumably Slatkin) mentioned a Hitachi, and they first wrote a deliberately bad upbeat song before turning to a sad one about intimacy fading in a relationship. The page puts its song headings after the quotes, so which track the anecdote belongs to is ambiguous; the Hitachi detail points to 'Hitachi'. Separately, via Teen Vogue as quoted by Just Jared, she says 'Hitachi' opens on a stack of harmonies.
quote: We were trying to write an upbeat song
why_it_matters: An off-topic joke in the room can become the title, and the song can then go the opposite way from the joke (sad, not cheeky), which gives the title an edge.
when_not: The Arts Desk (AD-S35 para 4) warned that a novelty title like this risks gimmickry and survives only if the song fully commits to its premise.

source: AD-S17#quoted paras 1-3; AD-S10#para 10; AD-S15#'The Event' paras 1-2
finding: ADÉLA says that while writing the album she watched Eyes Wide Shut and wanted more Nicole Kidman in it. At a Golden Globes party she felt she had no business attending, dressed up in a tight corset, she thought that she felt like Nicole Kidman. She sums the song up as being about feeling like Nicole, so the celebrity's name is a shorthand for a feeling, not a song about the actress. Sources disagree on the order of events (Capital puts the film the day before the party, Songfacts after) and on who first printed the quote (W Magazine or Rolling Stone).
quote: I feel like Nicole and that's what the song is about.
why_it_matters: A celebrity-name title works when the name stands for one specific feeling the narrator borrows (here, poised movie-star glamour), not when the song is about the celebrity.
when_not: NME (AD-S26 para 9) called it one of the album's few misses even as it became a UK top-5 single (AD-S50), so critics and listeners split on it.

source: AD-S20#exchange on Slovak background and family; AD-S37#Q&A on Slovak directness
finding: On NPR, ADÉLA calls herself a very blunt person, links that to a feistiness she sees in Eastern European women, and names her mother as the bluntest person she knows. She calls herself dry and sarcastic and says humour makes it easier to face things that aren't funny. In Vogue CS she contrasts Slovaks, who say it straight away, with Americans, who circle around the point. Taken together she presents bluntness as cultural and the joke as a way to carry hard material.
why_it_matters: A narrator who states the uncomfortable thing straight away, then undercuts it with dry humour, can get hard material across without sounding heavy.
when_not: Rolling Stone (AD-S24 paras 5, 8) found the stated, told-not-shown moments the weakest, so bluntness about feelings works less well than bluntness about facts.

finding: ADÉLA says 'Therapy' was recorded around Grammy week with her voice almost gone, with heavy Auto-Tune as a result. The first take ran about 15 minutes of her talking over the beat, and it was cut down to a three-minute track. She calls it more of a therapy session than a song; its subjects are frustration with executives, missing her younger sister and moving away. The song was edited down from a stream of consciousness rather than built from a sectioned draft.
quote: That was just rambling on the beat.
why_it_matters: Recording a long unfiltered ramble over the beat, then cutting it down, is one way to find the lines a sectioned draft would never produce.
when_not: Several reviewers found the result the album's weakest: lyrics 'especially simple' (AD-S47 para 10), hard to endure vocally (AD-S45 para 19), a slog (AD-S44 para 4), and the lowest user track score on AOTY (AD-S28). Diary material needs a strong edit.

finding: ADÉLA tells Vogue CS that 'KGB' was meant literally and partly as a joke, and that listeners who expected a metaphor were confused; she added an on-screen disclaimer in the video saying she supports Ukraine. W Magazine describes the song's persona as a fly on the wall absorbing American pop culture like a spy, with a lyric about learning English as a child. Learning English is therefore subject matter in the song. No fetched source has her discussing what it is like to write lyrics in her second language.
why_it_matters: A loaded political noun used as a comic, literal persona can be misread as a metaphor or a political statement, so the frame may need to be made explicit, as she did in the video.
when_not: Rolling Stone (AD-S24 para 5) felt 'KGB' tried too hard to convince, while Arts Desk (AD-S35 para 2) called it over the top but tightly written; the comic persona splits critics.

source: AD-S18#paras 7-10; AD-S12#para 2; AD-S37#Q&A on 'Ain't in LA'
finding: ADÉLA gives three linked sources for 'Ain't In LA'. The first is a photo of her mother at 18 in front of Western pop posters that her grandfather smuggled in from Germany. The second is Lorde's 'Royals' and 'Team', which meant a lot to her as a child and which she wanted to echo by writing about being outside the zeitgeist. The third is frustration, as someone who lives in LA, at the same people and beauty standards being praised. In Vogue CS she says LA in the title works as a metaphor, because she was tired of celebrity-focused songs.
quote: Where it's like being not in the zeitgeist, right?
why_it_matters: A place name can stand for a whole value system, and the song can define itself by refusing that place rather than describing it.
when_not: Some Singles Jukebox critics (AD-S36) heard the 'Royals' model as derivative, and St. Asaph found the outsider stance patronising.

source: AD-S13#subject matter and Theron Thomas sections; AD-S10#para 9; AD-S9#para 5
finding: Songfacts describes verse one as a run of small domestic details (a shared bedroom with a younger brother, hand-me-down clothes, Madonna and Destiny's Child posters), with verse two widening from one girl to girls in unknown cities everywhere. The title and chorus are built on a negation (where the cool ones are not). A pitched-down, distorted male refrain or intro is performed by Theron Thomas (W para 9; Songfacts calls it chopped and screwed and notes it recalls 'We Can't Stop', which he co-wrote). The FADER heard the effect as a nod to early A$AP Rocky and Bangerz-era Miley. Credited writers: Jergová, Walsh, Thomas, Slatkin, Brady (AD-S13, AD-S4).
why_it_matters: Moving from one specific girl in verse one to a crowd in verse two turns a personal memory into an anthem, and a second voice on the refrain can carry the song's period reference.
when_not: Whether Thomas wrote the refrain or only performs it is not established, and nothing about the chopped-and-screwed sound is verifiable here without audio.

source: AD-S36#blurbs: Kuppermann, Doyle, St. Asaph, Leah Isobel, Mathers, Varela, Alatorre
finding: Seventeen Singles Jukebox critics averaged 5.76/10 and split sharply. Kuppermann (4) said the lyrics are too vague because the only named place is Los Angeles; Doyle (5) wanted specific Bratislava detail and called it tasteful to the point of blandness; St. Asaph (3) found a line about smaller towns patronising. Mathers (10) called the chorus great, Varela (8) praised the shout-along hook, and Leah Isobel (6) heard the chorus's negation as leaving an unsettling gap. Reviewer view: the hook carries the song, while the abstraction that lets every listener in is also what costs it specificity.
quote: Everything here is one step too vague.
why_it_matters: If a song is about the places outside the famous city, naming at least one of them stops the outsider stance from feeling generic.
when_not: For a chart anthem the vagueness may be deliberate: it became her first Hot 100 entry and a UK No. 12 (AD-S49, AD-S50), so the critics' preference is not the audience's.

source: AD-S48#entry #4 'Boys'; AD-S46#para 5; AD-S16#quote block 4; AD-S4#track notes
finding: Reviewers describe 'Boys' as built around spoken exchanges between ADÉLA and KATSEYE's Lara Raj that break up the verses and choruses; Wikipedia lists her as uncredited. RatingsGameMusic says the lyric compares male attention to a vending machine, and Pipe Dream (AD-S47 para 8) reads the song as wanting yet resenting male attention. In the Capital write-up ADÉLA says the lyric is about men who hover around her and her friends on nights out without engaging, and that she brought Raj in because their conversations are very funny. That quote sits under the 'Red Bottoms' heading; that it belongs to 'Boys' is my inference.
why_it_matters: Dropping real friend-to-friend banter into the gaps between sections can deliver attitude and comedy that a sung line would make too earnest.
when_not: The Arts Desk (AD-S35 para 3) found 'Boys' too minimal to convey the carelessness it aimed for.

finding: Critics disagree on whether her voice works best with or without a wink. Rolling Stone's Larisha Paul says she sings with steady eye contact rather than a wink, that she convinces most when showing rather than telling, and that the predictable moments ('KGB' trying too hard, plodding 'Marijuana' lyrics, 'Starving Artist' near a Tate McRae throwaway) fall flat. NME's Bailey Slater says the opposite: she shines brightest when winking at pop's cheekier side, and 'KGB' is pastiche-laden. In her own words she pairs vulnerability with swagger (AD-S3 para 3) and calls her stage choreography campy, knowing and almost ironic (AD-S10 para 7), though that remark is about dance, not lyrics.
quote: Predictable doesn't really work for her
why_it_matters: Decide line by line whether the narrator is winking or deadpan; critics punished the moments that were neither and simply stated the obvious.
when_not: Critics' readings of tone do not show what the writers intended.

source: AD-S44#para 4; AD-S45#paras 11, 19, 21; AD-S47#paras 10, 12; AD-S35#paras 3, 5; AD-S23#para 4; AD-S26#para 9
finding: The recurring criticism is aimed at the slower, sincere songs. A Sputnik user reviewer (low weight) says she has not yet learned to write convincingly sincere lyrics and calls 'Hitachi' and 'Therapy' a slog; The Post says the album wears its influences too openly; The Arts Desk says 'Marijuana' repeats ideas from other tracks and that parts of the album are simple homage; Pipe Dream reports fans finding the album tamer and more on-the-nose than her provocative EP. Other critics disagree: Clash calls 'Hitachi' terrific and NME says 'Hitachi' and 'Therapy' capture the turmoil of first heartbreak. Metacritic's aggregate is mixed-to-favourable (AD-S27).
why_it_matters: An artist whose edge comes from cheek needs her sincere songs to keep a specific, unexpected image; plain diary statements are where critics lost interest.
when_not: Two credible outlets found the ballads the emotional peak, so this is a split verdict, not a consensus.

finding: ADÉLA tells Clash she used to avoid writing about love and that PRIMA pushed her into love songs, which she now treats as an important human experience. She says she wanted the album to cover love, family, sex and insecurity about sex, and to be witty, young and girly but also smart and deep. Clash also paraphrases advice from Slatkin and Brady that writing to what people want produces the worst art; this is the interviewer's paraphrase, not the producers' words. In the label press release she says she mixed the hard with the soft and the vulnerable with the swagger.
quote: I had an aversion to writing about love
why_it_matters: Pairing opposite registers on purpose (witty with deep, swagger with vulnerability) gives an album its range, and the topic a writer has avoided can be where the new material is.
when_not: No producer or co-writer statement was found to corroborate how the sessions actually ran.

source: AD-F1; AD-F3; AD-F4; AD-F7; AD-S35#para 4; AD-S50
finding: My inference: at least five of the eleven PRIMA titles are loaded proper nouns or brand-type names ('KGB', 'Nicole Kidman', 'Red Bottoms', 'Hitachi', 'Marijuana'). In every case where she explains the origin, the noun stands for an emotional state, not the topic: a corset moment means feeling like a movie star, a worn shoe means being run down, a session joke becomes a song about fading intimacy, a spy agency stands for an immigrant kid soaking up American culture. The noun gets attention and provokes, while the song underneath does something else. It worked commercially for 'Nicole Kidman' (UK No. 4) but drew 'gimmick risk' and 'miss' verdicts from critics.
why_it_matters: When pitching a proper-noun title in a session, check what feeling the noun stands for; if nobody can say, it is only a novelty.
when_not: No source has her or a co-writer describing this as a deliberate method; it is a pattern I see across her accounts.
